paragraphs: Simultaneous localization and mapping asks a robot to estimate its position while building a map of its surroundings. This paper addresses the version where measurements provide distances, with known correspondences specifying which measurements refer to which mapped objects. It introduces a spectral learning algorithm within a broader framework for identifying systems from data.

That framework gives the method statistical consistency and avoids local optima. The approach also does not require linearizing the motion or measurement model, a step used by several established filtering approaches. The authors provide finite-sample error bounds, connecting the theoretical analysis to the amount of available data, alongside guarantees of low computational requirements.

On a real robotic mapping problem, combining the spectral method with batch optimization produces the lowest errors among the compared methods. The spectral method alone performs nearly as well while requiring much less computation. These findings make the computational tradeoff concrete: the method offers useful tracking accuracy on its own, while its combination with batch optimization achieves the best accuracy in the reported comparison.
icml-2013-a-spectral-learning-approach-t.tldr: A spectral method estimates robot position and maps from distance measurements, combining theoretical guarantees with low computational cost.

paragraphs: Finding a target efficiently requires deciding where to look next and how much to spend on each observation. This paper studies a sequential search problem in which an imperfect classifier examines an interval. The decision includes the interval's location and length, as well as a choice of classifier cost and accuracy.

The authors express the problem in Bayesian terms, updating uncertainty about the target after each observation. Their objective combines the entropy of the resulting probability distribution with the accumulated cost of observations. For this formulation, they prove that choosing the best next observation through one-step lookahead is Bayes-optimal for any time horizon. A decision rule that considers just the immediate next step therefore achieves the full-horizon optimum in the studied problem.

The policy is also straightforward to calculate and implement. Applied to locating mitochondria in electron microscope images, it substantially speeds image acquisition relative to existing policies while preserving nearly equal image quality at target locations. This connects the optimality result to a practical allocation problem: concentrating acquisition effort where the desired structures are located.
icml-2013-an-optimal-policy-for-target-l.tldr: For a Bayesian target-search formulation, a simple one-step policy is optimal and speeds microscopy acquisition while preserving target-region image quality.

paragraphs: This paper develops a cheaper way to run the Frank-Wolfe algorithm on convex problems whose constraints separate into blocks. Instead of performing the full update at every iteration, the proposed method randomly selects a block to update. The central question is whether this reduction in work per iteration preserves useful progress toward the optimum.

The authors show that the randomized method achieves a similar convergence rate to full Frank-Wolfe when measured by the duality gap. That gap provides a certificate of how far the current solution may be from optimality. Applied to the dual formulation of a structural support vector machine, the method becomes an online algorithm with iteration costs comparable to primal stochastic subgradient methods.

The resulting solver also supports an optimal step-size calculation and a computable duality-gap guarantee. These features provide both a principled update size and a way to assess remaining optimization error. Experiments indicate that the algorithm outperforms competing structural SVM solvers, supporting the practical value of combining inexpensive updates with an explicit measure of solution quality.
icml-2013-block-coordinate-frank-wolfe-o.tldr: Randomized block updates make Frank-Wolfe inexpensive for structural SVMs while retaining convergence guarantees and a computable optimality certificate.

paragraphs: Domain generalization concerns using knowledge from several related data sources to make predictions on a previously unseen source. The challenge is to find features that remain useful when the domain changes. This paper proposes Domain-Invariant Component Analysis, or DICA, to learn a transformation that reduces differences between the available domains.

DICA uses a kernel-based optimization procedure with two linked aims: make domains less dissimilar and preserve the relationship between inputs and outputs. Preserving that relationship matters because removing domain differences alone could also remove information needed for prediction. The learned representation therefore seeks common structure that still supports the predictive task.

A learning-theoretic analysis connects reduced domain dissimilarity with improved expected generalization to new domains, providing motivation for the optimization objective. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that DICA learns invariant features and improves classifier performance. Together, these results support treating representation learning as a balance between reducing domain-specific variation and retaining the information that links examples to their labels.
icml-2013-domain-generalization-via-inva.tldr: DICA learns predictive features that reduce differences across related domains, improving generalization to unseen domains in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is attractive because each update is inexpensive and can tolerate noisy gradient information. Its progress, however, depends on the local scaling of the objective. This paper investigates how to use curvature information to improve optimization while retaining computational costs suitable for problems with many input dimensions.

The Hessian describes local curvature and provides the scaling used by Newton-Raphson optimization. Obtaining and using that information can be costly, especially when gradient evaluations are noisy. The authors construct a nonparametric Bayesian quasi-Newton algorithm that learns both the gradient and the Hessian from noisy gradient observations, making uncertainty part of the estimation process.

The resulting algorithm has computational cost linear in the number of input dimensions, matching the dimensional scaling highlighted for stochastic gradient descent. Its contribution is thus a way to incorporate learned curvature without the super-linear expense associated with existing covariant approaches discussed in the abstract. The comparison with Newton's method motivates the use of curvature; the stated result establishes the construction and its computational scaling.
icml-2013-fast-probabilistic-optimizatio.tldr: A Bayesian quasi-Newton algorithm learns curvature from noisy gradients while keeping computational cost linear in the input dimension.

paragraphs: Multi-fold cross-validation estimates a learning algorithm's error by combining evaluations across several training and validation splits. Understanding how much this combination reduces variability is difficult because the folds introduce correlations. The estimates cannot simply be treated as independent measurements, so their dependence must be accounted for in a useful theoretical analysis.

This paper introduces a weak notion of stability called loss stability and relates it to cross-validation performance. The idea is to connect the reliability of the error estimate with a property of the learning algorithm's losses. This gives the analysis a way to characterize cross-validation beyond merely counting how many folds are averaged.

The authors establish that the relationship is near-optimal and use it to improve the best existing quantitative bounds. The contribution is a sharper theoretical account of cross-validation's variance-reduction benefits. It explains those benefits through loss stability while addressing the correlations that make the problem challenging, rather than assuming that repeated evaluations automatically deliver the gains of independent observations.
icml-2013-near-optimal-bounds-for-cross-.tldr: A weak loss-stability condition yields sharper, near-optimal bounds on cross-validation performance despite correlations between folds.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering organizes unlabeled points according to the low-dimensional subspaces underlying them. The setting assumes that the clean data lie in a union of such subspaces, so different groups can follow different low-dimensional structures. This paper examines what happens when noise perturbs those points and obscures the structure the clustering method should recover.

The authors analyze Sparse Subspace Clustering under both adversarial and random noise. These are distinct ways of modeling corruption, and considering both broadens the theoretical treatment beyond a single noise mechanism. They show that a modified version of the algorithm can provably identify the underlying subspaces correctly in the noisy settings they study.

The contribution extends the algorithm's theoretical justification to data that are imperfectly observed. This matters because success on ideal subspace data alone would not explain why the method can remain useful when observations contain disturbances. The result supports SSC's effectiveness for a class of real applications while retaining the central modeling assumption that the underlying clean points belong to low-dimensional subspaces.
icml-2013-noisy-sparse-subspace-clusteri.tldr: A modified Sparse Subspace Clustering algorithm has recovery guarantees for the studied settings with adversarial or random noise.

paragraphs: This paper develops a sparse version of uncorrelated linear discriminant analysis, a method for transforming data into a representation useful for distinguishing classes. Sparsity makes the transformation depend on relatively few coefficients. The authors seek this property while working within the solution set of generalized uncorrelated linear discriminant analysis.

Their starting point is a characterization of all solutions to the generalized problem. Among those with minimum dimension, they select the solution with the smallest sum of absolute coefficient values, or l1 norm. This turns the search for a sparse transformation into an l1-minimization problem, which they solve using an accelerated linearized Bregman method.

Experiments on high-dimensional gene expression data produce extremely sparse solutions while maintaining good classification performance. The results also demonstrate usefulness for visualizing data in a low-dimensional space. These findings show how the same transformation can support prediction and visual inspection: it compresses the representation, uses few coefficients, and retains information that helps separate the observed classes.
icml-2013-sparse-uncorrelated-linear-dis.tldr: Selecting a minimum-l1 solution within generalized ULDA yields very sparse transformations that support classification and low-dimensional visualization.

paragraphs: Predictive sparse coding represents an example using a small selection of dictionary elements, then applies a linear predictor to that representation. Both the representation and its usefulness for prediction matter. This paper studies why such a learned system should perform well beyond its training examples, focusing on dictionaries with more features than the original input dimension.

The authors establish generalization-error bounds for this overcomplete setting. The stated dependence on input dimension d, dictionary size k, and sample count m scales as the square root of d times k divided by m. Holding the dimensions fixed, this part of the bound decreases as more training examples become available.

The bound also depends closely on the learned encoder's stability, assessed on the training sample. To support the analysis, the paper proves a stability result for LASSO that characterizes how sparse codes respond to changes in the dictionary. This connects prediction on unseen data to the robustness of the representation itself: the theory tracks how dictionary perturbations affect the codes used by the predictor.
icml-2013-sparsity-based-generalization-.tldr: Generalization bounds for overcomplete predictive sparse coding connect sample size and representation dimensions with the stability of learned sparse codes.

paragraphs: Large-scale and distributed learning motivate optimization methods that can handle objectives composed of multiple parts. This paper introduces a stochastic formulation for problems with convex, nonsmooth composite objectives and develops a stochastic version of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM, to solve them.

The algorithm covers a broader class of objectives than the smooth, separable least-squares loss used in lasso. Its analysis gives convergence rates under different structural assumptions: O(1/sqrt(t)) for convex functions and O(log(t)/t) for strongly convex functions. These rates distinguish how much progress can be guaranteed as the number of iterations grows under each assumption.

The guarantees address both the objective value and feasibility violation, meaning the extent to which the solution fails to satisfy the problem's constraints. Tracking both quantities matters because reducing the objective alone does not establish that a constrained solution is acceptable. The authors also propose a Graph-Guided SVM application to demonstrate the algorithm's usefulness, linking the general optimization framework to a concrete learning problem.
icml-2013-stochastic-alternating-directi.tldr: Stochastic ADMM handles convex nonsmooth composite objectives with convergence guarantees covering both objective quality and constraint violations.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives, including those used in support vector machines, are nonsmooth. Classical analyses of stochastic gradient descent often rely on smoothness assumptions that do not cover these objectives. This paper studies SGD without those assumptions and separates two questions: how good its final iterate is, and how averaging iterates can improve accuracy.

After T iterations, the authors bound the final iterate's suboptimality by O(log(T)/sqrt(T)) for convex objectives and O(log(T)/T) for strongly convex objectives. Suboptimality measures the remaining difference from the best objective value. These bounds nearly match the minimax-optimal rates available through appropriate averaging, clarifying what can be guaranteed when simply using the last update.

The paper also introduces a simple running average that attains optimal rates and can be maintained during optimization. This makes the theoretical benefit of averaging easier to implement than the suffix-averaging approach discussed in the abstract. Experimental illustrations accompany the analysis, while the main contribution is the combination of final-iterate guarantees and an easily computed, optimally accurate averaging scheme.
icml-2013-stochastic-gradient-descent-fo.tldr: For nonsmooth convex optimization, the paper bounds SGD's final-iterate error and introduces a simple running average with optimal rates.

paragraphs: Neural network verification often divides a difficult problem into smaller regions using branch-and-bound, then computes bounds within each region. The number of resulting subproblems can become a major computational burden. This paper proposes using linear constraints already available during verification to reduce the regions and tighten the bounds being examined.

The framework contains two algorithms. One removes portions of the input space that are already verified or irrelevant to the current subdomain; the other directly improves intermediate bounds inside the network. The procedures use those constraints more scalably than off-the-shelf linear programming solvers and can integrate with verifiers such as alpha-beta-CROWN, including schemes that branch on inputs or activations.

Reducing the domain can tighten bounds throughout the network and decrease the amount of branching needed. Across the reported benchmarks, some instances show a 96% reduction in subproblem count, and the approach achieves state-of-the-art verified accuracy on multiple benchmarks. The result demonstrates that information already produced by verification can be used more effectively to reduce subsequent work.
neurips-2025-clip-and-verify-linear-cons.tldr: Using existing linear constraints to clip verification domains tightens bounds and, in some benchmark instances, reduces branch-and-bound subproblems by 96%.

paragraphs: Causal effect estimation asks what would happen under an intervention, which differs from predicting what is normally observed. Existing approaches can require intervention data, knowledge of the causal graph, or assumptions such as the absence of confounding. This paper investigates whether prior-data fitted networks can transfer their success in tabular prediction to this causal task.

The authors pretrain these networks on synthetic data generated from a wide variety of causal structures, including interventions. The training objective is to predict interventional outcomes when given observational data. This setup exposes the network to relationships between observations and interventions during pretraining, then uses in-context learning to address the estimation problem.

Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings show accurate causal-effect estimation without supplying the underlying causal graph. The evidence supports the usefulness of learning across diverse simulated causal structures for the tested tasks. The distinction between training and application is central: intervention information appears in the synthetic pretraining process, while the desired prediction is made from observational data without knowledge of the true graph.
neurips-2025-do-pfn-in-context-learning-.tldr: Do-PFN learns from synthetic causal structures to estimate intervention effects from observational data without a supplied causal graph in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Data attribution estimates how a model's predictions would change if its training dataset changed. Computing these estimates can require substantial resources, creating a trust problem when others must rely on the results. This paper proposes an interactive protocol in which a powerful, untrusted prover supplies attributions to a verifier with fewer resources.

The protocol provides formal guarantees in a probably-approximately-correct framework. When both parties follow it, the verifier accepts attributions within epsilon of optimal mean squared error with probability at least one minus delta. A prover that deviates arbitrarily, even with unlimited computation, is detected or still provides attributions to the verifier, except with probability delta.

The verifier's required number of independent model retrainings scales as O(1/epsilon²), independently of dataset size. This targets the expensive part of checking attribution quality and separates verification effort from the size of the training collection. The underlying result covers verification of linear functions over the Boolean hypercube, giving the protocol relevance to multiple attribution tasks beyond a single application.
neurips-2025-efficiently-verifiable-proo.tldr: An interactive proof lets a resource-constrained verifier check data attributions with formal guarantees and a retraining count independent of dataset size.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization reduces fine-tuning memory requirements by estimating gradients through forward passes, avoiding backward passes. Its appeal is constrained by slower convergence and weaker accuracy than first-order optimization. This paper studies how the two approaches update different layers and uses those differences to design a more effective zeroth-order method.

The proposed DiZO optimizer adapts updates separately for each layer. Guided by a layer-wise divergence analysis, it applies projections that produce update magnitudes matched to individual layers' optimization needs. The aim is to recover more of the learning capacity associated with first-order training while retaining the forward-pass-based approach.

Across the reported datasets, DiZO reduces the iterations needed for convergence without sacrificing throughput, cutting training GPU hours by up to 48%. It consistently outperforms the representative zeroth-order baselines for RoBERTa-large, OPT, and Llama fine-tuning tasks, and sometimes exceeds first-order fine-tuning performance. These results suggest that adjusting how updates are distributed across layers can improve both training efficiency and downstream accuracy within the tested settings.
neurips-2025-harmony-in-divergence-towar.tldr: DiZO adapts zeroth-order updates by layer, improving reported fine-tuning accuracy and reducing training GPU hours by up to 48%.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn meaningful patterns and memorize irrelevant variation in the same training set. When the signal is weak relative to the noise, memorization can dominate and hurt predictions on new data. This paper investigates whether deliberately adding label noise to gradient updates can help prevent that outcome.

The analysis studies a two-layer neural network in an idealized setting that separates signal and noise. The authors prove that their label-noise gradient descent procedure suppresses noise memorization while allowing the signal to grow rapidly. Within this setting, overfitting stays controlled and the network achieves good generalization despite the low signal-to-noise ratio.

The paper also analyzes ordinary gradient descent under the same conditions. It shows a tendency to overfit noise and establishes a test-error lower bound that does not vanish. This comparison identifies a theoretical mechanism for the benefit of injected label noise: it changes the balance between learning useful structure and fitting noise. The guarantee concerns the specified network and data model, making those assumptions integral to interpreting the result.
neurips-2025-how-does-label-noise-gradie.tldr: In an idealized two-layer network setting, label-noise gradient descent suppresses noise memorization and improves generalization when the signal is weak.

paragraphs: Continual learning must balance acquiring new tasks with retaining earlier knowledge. Pretrained models can help preserve useful representations, but the choice of a single backbone can restrict adaptation. This paper builds a framework that combines several different pretrained backbones to obtain richer representations from multiple sources.

Its Multi-Scale Interaction and Dynamic Fusion component uses learnable attention modules to select relevant information from the different feature sources. A Multi-Level Representation Optimization strategy then adapts the representation networks to improve their capacity to learn new tasks. Together, these components address both which features to use and how those features should change.

The framework also introduces Adaptive Regularization Optimization, which controls a switch vector governing updates to individual representation layers. This is designed to reduce excessive regularization that would otherwise hinder new learning. Joint optimization coordinates adaptation and preservation, and the reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance. The approach treats continual learning as a problem of selecting, refining, and selectively updating representations across multiple pretrained sources.
neurips-2025-learning-multi-source-and-r.tldr: Combining multiple pretrained backbones with selective feature fusion and layer adaptation improves the reported balance between learning new tasks and preserving knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples are needed to recover some information about the relevant subspace in a Gaussian multi-index model. The goal is weak reconstruction: obtaining a direction that correlates with that subspace. These models provide a setting for studying computational questions about neural networks, but extending results beyond a single index has been difficult.

The authors construct spectral algorithms by linearizing a message-passing scheme tailored to the problem. Their main result shows that the proposed methods attain the optimal reconstruction threshold. A high-dimensional analysis identifies what happens above that threshold: the leading eigenvector becomes correlated with the relevant index subspace.

This change resembles a spectral transition in spiked random-matrix models, where an informative direction emerges once the signal becomes detectable. Rigorous analysis and numerical experiments support the result. The contribution pinpoints a sample threshold for weak learning in the studied Gaussian multi-index setting and provides algorithms that reach it, connecting an abstract learnability boundary to a concrete eigenvector-based procedure.
neurips-2025-optimal-spectral-transition.tldr: Spectral algorithms derived from message passing achieve the optimal weak-reconstruction threshold in the studied Gaussian multi-index setting.

paragraphs: Visually convincing generated videos can still contain subtle inconsistencies in how their content changes over space and time. This paper proposes detecting those inconsistencies through a framework based on probability-flow conservation. Its central statistic, the Normalized Spatiotemporal Gradient, compares spatial probability gradients with temporal density changes to characterize departures from natural video dynamics.

The authors estimate this statistic using pretrained diffusion models, combining approximate spatial gradients with motion-aware temporal modeling. This avoids complex motion decomposition while preserving the framework's physical constraints. The detector then compares the resulting features for test videos and real videos using Maximum Mean Discrepancy, turning differences between feature distributions into a detection score.

The paper also derives an upper bound on feature distances and establishes amplified discrepancies associated with distributional shifts in generated videos. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines of 16.00% in recall and 10.75% in F1 score. The approach's significance lies in measuring the consistency of video dynamics, providing a detection signal beyond the apparent realism of individual frames.
neurips-2025-physics-driven-spatiotempor.tldr: A probability-flow-based statistic detects spatial and temporal inconsistencies in generated videos, improving recall and F1 in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single image can produce a depth map that looks plausible yet creates stray points around edges when converted into a point cloud. This paper attributes such flying-pixel artifacts in existing generative approaches to compressing depth maps through a variational autoencoder. Pixel-Perfect Depth instead performs diffusion directly in pixel space.

Direct generation avoids the identified compression artifacts but increases computational complexity. The model addresses this with two designs. Semantics-Prompted Diffusion Transformers use representations from vision foundation models to guide generation, maintaining global semantic consistency while improving fine details. A cascaded transformer design progressively increases the token count to improve efficiency and accuracy.

The authors report the best performance among published generative models across five benchmarks and significant gains over all other models in edge-aware point-cloud evaluation. The model also produces point clouds described as free of flying pixels. These findings connect the choice of generation space to the geometry of the output: preserving depth boundaries matters when an estimated map becomes a three-dimensional collection of points.
neurips-2025-pixel-perfect-depth-with-se.tldr: Pixel-space diffusion guided by semantic features improves monocular depth estimation and avoids the VAE-induced flying pixels described in the paper.

paragraphs: Text-to-vision models can produce highly realistic outputs while struggling to express unusual concepts in a prompt. This paper investigates whether rare meanings can be brought out through a small intervention inside multimodal diffusion transformers. The method requires no additional training, new data, denoising-time optimization, or external language model.

The intervention targets the text embeddings processed by joint-attention blocks. In these models, text and image embeddings are updated together throughout the transformer. The authors increase the variance of text-token embeddings before joint attention, describing this as expanding the representational regions around those tokens. They find that this adjustment makes rare semantics more apparent in generated outputs.

The reported results extend across text-to-image generation, text-to-video generation, and text-guided image editing. This suggests that the intervention addresses a mechanism shared across several text-conditioned visual tasks. The contribution is a way to expose meanings already represented within the model through a change to its internal text representations, with demonstrated improvements across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-rare-text-semantics-were-al.tldr: Scaling text-embedding variance before joint attention helps multimodal diffusion transformers express rare prompt concepts without additional training.

paragraphs: Subspace Networks addresses a communication problem in decentralized model training: moving information between devices can become a bottleneck. In data parallelism, devices exchange weight gradients. Model parallelism instead requires exchanging activations and their gradients as computation moves through layers. Compressing these signals can introduce errors that accumulate, so compression methods effective for data parallelism do not directly carry over.

The paper proposes compressing communication during both the forward and backward passes. Its central idea uses a recursive structure in transformer networks to predefine a low-dimensional subspace that contains the activations and gradients. This provides a compact representation while allowing full reconstruction in subsequent layers, addressing the accumulation of compression errors.

The authors report up to 99% compression without degraded convergence and with negligible additional memory or computation. They also report up to a 100-fold improvement in communication efficiency. These are stated maximum gains, showing how substantially the method can reduce communication requirements.

The method enables billion-parameter-scale training on low-end GPUs using consumer internet connections as slow as 80 Mbps. The authors report convergence matching centralized datacenter model-parallel training with 100 Gbps connections. This finding supports the possibility of training large models across devices with much slower network links; the stated comparison concerns convergence, rather than equal training time.
neurips-2025-subspace-networks-scaling-d.tldr: Subspace Networks compresses transformer activations and gradients to enable decentralized billion-parameter training over slow internet connections while reporting convergence matching centralized model-parallel training.

paragraphs: This paper studies how large the expected value of a ranked extreme can become as the number of independent, identically distributed samples grows. It assumes the sampling distribution has finite expectation. The main distinction is between the largest observation and any fixed lower rank, such as the second largest.

For the maximum, the known tight growth characterization is o(n). For any fixed rank greater than one, the authors establish an upper growth bound of O(n/(log(n) log(log(n)))) and a lower bound of Omega(n/(log(n) (log(log(n)))^1.01)). They also provide a finer characterization of achievable growth. The result shows that moving just below the maximum changes the extreme expectation's possible growth substantially.

Simulations highlight a difference between expectation-driven extremes and typical outcomes. Although the multiplicative gap between the maximum and second maximum grows quickly with sample count, their ratio stays approximately constant in 99% of trials. This suggests that sharp worst-case growth can coexist with much steadier typical behavior, a distinction relevant to applications that depend on extreme observations.
neurips-2025-tight-asymptotics-of-extrem.tldr: Under finite expectation, fixed-ranked extremes below the maximum have sharply different growth bounds, while simulations show steadier typical ratios.

paragraphs: Novel view synthesis creates images from camera positions absent from a sparse collection of observed views. Visible parts of a scene can support direct rendering, while hidden regions require plausible completion. UMAMI combines these capabilities to address the blur associated with deterministic rendering and the high computational cost of fully generative approaches.

A bidirectional transformer encodes image tokens from multiple views together with ray representations describing their viewing geometry. Two lightweight heads use the shared representation. A feed-forward regression head renders pixels where geometry is well constrained, while a masked autoregressive diffusion head completes occluded or unseen content. The model is trained jointly with photometric and diffusion losses, without handcrafted three-dimensional inductive biases.

Experiments report state-of-the-art image quality and an order-of-magnitude reduction in rendering time compared with fully generative baselines. The architectural division makes the reason for the efficiency gain clear: direct prediction and generative completion serve different parts of the rendering problem. A shared representation lets the model coordinate those functions within a single end-to-end training framework.
neurips-2025-umami-unifying-masked-autor.tldr: UMAMI combines direct rendering with generative completion, achieving strong view-synthesis quality and an order-of-magnitude rendering speedup over fully generative baselines.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with coverage guarantees. In practice, several models or methods may each provide a valid set, creating a natural desire to choose the most useful one. This paper addresses a subtle problem: selecting among individually valid sets, for example by choosing the smallest, can destroy the coverage guarantee.

The authors propose a stability-based approach that ensures coverage for the selected prediction set. The key contribution is to account for the selection step itself. Having a guarantee for every candidate separately is insufficient to justify the final choice, so the method makes validity after selection the object of the analysis.

The results also extend to online conformal prediction, and the paper develops refinements for settings with additional structure. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. This work matters whenever practical preferences guide a choice among prediction sets: it provides a way to accommodate that choice while retaining a coverage guarantee, rather than evaluating validity only before the selection takes place.
neurips-2025-valid-selection-among-confo.tldr: A stability-based method preserves conformal coverage when choosing among multiple prediction sets, including extensions to online settings.
